A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LingoLoop research. Their main text, equations, algorithms, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial appendix expansion and renumbering.

before.justification: V1 reports original attack experiments measuring generated tokens, energy consumption, and latency, together with ablations, prompt-transfer tests, and cross-model transfer results.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds multilingual experiments, commercial-model transfer, weight-pool analyses, and defense evaluations.

M1.justification: The core losses, PGD optimization, and Algorithm 1 are retained. Appendix D.6.2 adds an evaluated bilingual weight-pool variant using NLTK for English, jieba for Chinese, and a unified POS tagset. This is a limited adaptation of prior construction; the newly specified weighting formula alone does not establish a change to the original attack procedure.

E1.justification: MS-COCO and ImageNet remain the image datasets. V2 substantially expands linguistic coverage through Chinese, French, and Japanese evaluation and an English–Chinese caption pool. It also adds commercial API attack scenarios and text-only versus multimodal attack-attribution evaluations.

E2.justification: The attack-comparison baselines remain clean inputs, random noise where applicable, and Verbose Images. Defense comparisons expand substantially beyond decoding controls: Appendix F evaluates hidden-state monitoring, n-gram filtering, GPT-4o/Gemini judges, GuardReasoner-VL Eco-3B/Eco-7B, and Llama Guard 3 Vision.

E3.justification: The main 200-image evaluations and PGD settings are retained. New protocols include commercial API evaluation on 50 images using word counts, cross-architecture transfer, bilingual pool controls, and defense detection/attribution procedures. Top-p sampling is newly tested; Table 13 lists 0.2, 0.7, and 1.0, although its surrounding prose inconsistently states an upper value of 0.9.

E4.justification: V2 adds weight-pool sampling sensitivity and source-model transfer analyses, multilingual transfer and pool ablations, top-p sensitivity, and extensive defense analyses. These test substantive new questions about linguistic generalization, component specificity, stochastic decoding, and detectability. The earlier token-limit, prompt, perturbation-budget, and temperature analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Table 7 newly reports weight-pool data-sampling seeds: default, 1, 2, and 256. This adds explicit seed-sensitivity evidence, without establishing increased repeated runs of the main benchmarks. No run-level confidence intervals or significance tests are added for those benchmarks.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results across the new experiments. Figure 11b reports 287.9 tokens for cross-architecture LingoLoop transfer versus 231.2 for Verbose Images; Figure 12 reports 56.6 versus 46.1 words on GPT-4o and 144.5 versus 110.7 on Gemini 2.5 Pro. These are new comparisons, not improvements over v1 under identical settings. The original main scores and Table 5's approximately 367-fold result are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix B.3 adds Equation 11, explicitly defining the previously abstract prior-to-weight mapping as the EOS prior plus a 10^-10 stabilizer, multiplied by theta_w. This is a limited addition to mathematical specification. The existing objectives and optimization equations remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the 30-fold headline with approximately 367-fold token amplification when generation limits are relaxed. This promotes a result already reported in v1 Table 5 into the main contribution statement. The two central methodological contributions and the conclusion's overall claim remain substantially unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds economic threat scenarios, explanations of transfer-based practicality, shared cross-linguistic vulnerabilities, and an attribution/content-safety blind spot in defenses. It removes v1 Appendix E's substantive discussion of transfer limitations, architectural heterogeneity, and GPU-memory constraints, together with the earlier qualification that cross-model efficacy remains unsatisfactory relative to white-box attacks.

D1.justification: Reproducibility information expands through the exact weighting function and stabilizer, bilingual corpus construction and POS-processing libraries, defense thresholds, and complete judge prompts. These provide implementation information for both the existing attack and substantial new analyses. Main model preprocessing, hardware, and attack hyperparameters are retained; code release remains a future commitment rather than a supplied access link.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to GuardReasoner-VL and Llama Guard 3 Vision for the new defense evaluations, and removes the Schaeffer et al. transferability reference alongside the limitations discussion. The main related-work narrative and positioning against Verbose Images remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. V2 condenses selected passages, reverses the two Section 4.4 ablation discussions, reorganizes the appendices, moves Broader Impacts into an Ethics Statement, and adds reproducibility and LLM-use statements. Author-affiliation information is also expanded.

P2.justification: V2 adds ten tables and the commercial-transfer Figure 12, and expands Figure 11 into two source-model panels. The original qualitative Figures 12–15 are retained as Figures 13–16. The ICLR formatting, boxed prompts, resized figures, and rearranged tables produce substantial visual and layout changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: The multilingual and weight-pool controls answer previously untested mechanism questions, broader transfer tests strengthen generalization evidence, and the explicit weighting formula closes a reproducibility gap. These are useful quality gains. However, v2 removes substantive limitations and makes sweeping defense-failure claims partly from causal-attribution and content-safety classifications, which do not directly establish whether excess computation can be prevented. Those weaknesses temper the overall improvement; the stronger 367-fold headline itself reflects existing evidence.
